children.text: Siberut is the largest of the Mentawai Islands and the one almost nobody stops for. The other islands in the chain get the surf charters and the resort transfers, booked a year out and priced accordingly. Siberut gets a passenger ferry three mornings a week, a national park across its western half, and four primates that live nowhere else on earth.

That ferry is the whole trip. It sails on fixed days in both directions, so a Siberut plan is built backwards from a calendar rather than forwards from a wish list. Get the days wrong and you lose three of them waiting on a jetty. Get them right and nine days is enough to reach the inland valleys, sleep several nights in an uma, and still leave a buffer for the sea to have an opinion.

This is a slow, humid, muddy route with no restaurants, no scooters and no plan B on the water. What it has instead is a rainforest that has been separated from Sumatra for half a million years, and families who still live along the rivers of the Rereiket and host visitors who make the effort to get there.
Who this trip is for, and who should skip it

This route suits travellers who are comfortable being wet, walking in mud for hours, and sleeping on a wooden floor without power. It rewards curiosity about forest ecology and about how people live in it, and it asks for patience with a ferry that answers to the weather. Small groups of friends and confident solo travellers do best here.
It works well as a second or third Indonesian trip. If you have already done
Bali and the Gilis
and want something that is genuinely difficult to reach, this is the step up. It also pairs naturally with the Minangkabau highlands, because both trips start and end at the same airport.

Skip it if you need daily data coverage, a private bathroom, or a fixed return date you cannot move. Skip it if the appeal is photographs of tattooed elders rather than the island itself, because that framing tends to produce a bad trip for everyone involved. Families with young children should look at our
9-day north Sumatra route
instead, which delivers rainforest and wildlife with far gentler logistics.
Trip at a glance
Route:
Padang to Muara Siberut by ferry, upriver into the Rereiket valley, back to Muara Siberut, ferry to Padang.
Shape:
Two nights in Padang at the start and end, one night at the Siberut port on each side, three nights inland in an uma.
Ferry days:
Out on a Saturday, back on a Thursday. Those are the two sailings that make a nine-day trip fit without dead time.
Pace:
Slow, with two long boat days and three days of walking between four and seven hours in forest.
Best months:
There is no dry season worth the name on Siberut. Rain falls year round, and the practical variable is the sea state on the crossing, which is generally calmer between April and October.
Working budget:

Roughly USD 700 to 1,100 per person for the nine days excluding international flights, most of it the guided inland section. Prices change, so treat this as a planning figure and confirm before you commit.
Why this route makes sense

Siberut splits into two trips that share a port. The western half is national park and river valleys reached by canoe and on foot. The eastern coast is villages, a small town and the ferry. Almost everything worth the journey sits inland, and the only way in is by outboard canoe up rivers that shrink as you climb.

So the route commits to one thing properly. It uses the Rereiket river system southwest of Muara Siberut, which is the area with the most established hosting arrangements and the shortest transfer from the port, and it spends three nights there rather than trying to add a second region. Splitting the island in nine days would mean two more boat days and nothing gained.

The Padang bookends are not padding. Flights into Minangkabau are routinely delayed, and the ferry does not wait. A night in Padang before a sailing day converts a missed connection from a ruined trip into an inconvenience, and the same night on the way home does the same job in reverse.
How do you actually get to Siberut?

You fly to Padang in West Sumatra, then take the Mentawai Fast passenger ferry from the city to Muara Siberut. The operator publishes Siberut sailings on Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday, leaving around seven in the morning and taking roughly five to six hours with a stop at Sikabaluan. There is no airport on Siberut and no other scheduled way across.

Padang is well connected domestically. Jakarta to Padang runs dozens of times a day on Batik Air, Citilink, Garuda, Lion Air, Pelita Air and Super Air Jet, with fares starting around IDR 550,000 one way and a flying time under two hours; you can
compare Jakarta to Padang flights

to see the day's spread. Minangkabau International sits about 23 kilometres northwest of the city, and the Minangkabau Express train into town costs around Rp 10,000 while the Damri bus is around Rp 25,000, both as working estimates.

Ferry tickets for foreign passengers run somewhere around Rp 350,000 to Rp 400,000 each way depending on class and route, based on the fares operators publish. Buy at least a day ahead. Sailings are cancelled for weather with little notice, so check the operator's own channels the evening before rather than trusting a schedule you read weeks earlier.

children.text: Day 1: Fly into Padang and do nothing with the evening
Afternoon.

Land at Minangkabau, take the airport train or a car into the city, and check in near the seafront. Do not book anything demanding for today. This day exists so that a delayed flight cannot cost you the Saturday ferry.
Evening.

Eat properly, because it is the last restaurant meal for a week. Padang food is served by covering the table in small dishes and charging for what you touch, and rendang here bears little resemblance to the version served elsewhere.
Base:
Padang city, close to the coast road.
Rooms in Padang
are inexpensive and plentiful, and staying central is worth more than staying near the airport.
Booking logic:
Book the room, not a tour. The inland guiding is arranged separately and is the one thing that genuinely needs to be locked in advance.
Travel note:
Draw cash today. There is an ATM in Muara Siberut but it is a single point of failure, and nothing upriver takes cards.
Day 2: A Padang day, deliberately
Morning.

The Adityawarman Museum, built in the horned Minangkabau roof style, is a useful hour before you go anywhere near the Mentawai. It gives you the mainland context that the islands deliberately sit outside of.
Afternoon.
Walk the old town and the riverside godowns near Muaro, or take the short crossing to Air Manis beach. Neither is a spectacle. Both are pleasant and cost almost nothing.
Evening.
Pack for wet. Everything you carry inland should be inside a dry bag or two, and anything you would be upset to lose should stay in Padang. Most guesthouses will hold a bag for free.
Base:
Padang, same room.
Booking logic:
Buy the ferry ticket today, in person or through your guide, for tomorrow morning.
Travel note:
Coverage on Siberut is patchy and disappears entirely upriver. An
Indonesia eSIM from Airalo
will work in Padang and around the port town, and nowhere useful after that, which is worth knowing before you promise anyone a daily message.
Day 3: The morning ferry to Muara Siberut
Morning.

An early start for a seven o'clock sailing. The crossing runs roughly five to six hours with a stop, and the open water in the middle is the part that decides whether you enjoy it. Sit low and central if you are prone to seasickness, and take something before you board rather than after.
Afternoon.

Arrive at Muara Siberut in the early afternoon. It is a small port town of stilt houses, a market and a mosque, and an hour of walking covers it. Meet your guide, confirm the plan and buy anything the family will not have, which usually means sugar, coffee, tobacco and batteries.
Evening.
Simple guesthouse, early night. Tomorrow starts on the water.
Base:
Muara Siberut.
Booking logic:

Agree the full price of the inland days now, in writing, including how many nights, how many guides and porters, and what the host family receives directly. This conversation is much harder to have upriver.
Travel note:
Rubber boots are the single most useful thing you can carry, and they are sold cheaply in the market here. Buy a pair a size large so you can wear thick socks.
Day 4: Upriver into the Rereiket, and the first night in an uma
Morning.

A short road transfer, then a long outboard canoe up the Rereiket. The river narrows as you climb and the canopy closes over it. This is the best wildlife window of the trip, and hornbills and macaques are common along the banks.
Afternoon.

Leave the canoe and walk in. The trail is mud, log bridges and roots, and the walking time depends entirely on how much rain fell overnight. Two to four hours is normal. Arrive at the uma, the clan longhouse, in the late afternoon.
Evening.
Sit with the household while dinner is cooked over the fire. Do not expect a performance. The evening is quiet, dark by six, and the conversation runs through your guide.
Base:
An uma in the Rereiket valley, sleeping on a mat on the floor under a mosquito net.
Booking logic:
Nothing to book. Everything from here was arranged yesterday.
Travel note:
Ask before photographing anyone, every time, and accept no as an answer. A visit that people are relaxed about is worth more than any picture.
Day 5: A full day in the forest
Morning.

Out before dawn if you want to hear the bilou, the Kloss's gibbon, which calls at first light and is far easier to hear than to see. Siberut has four primates that exist nowhere else, and all four are listed as Endangered or Critically Endangered.
Afternoon.

The working day of the household: felling and processing a sago palm, checking traps and fishing lines, gathering forest plants. This is the part of the trip people remember, and it is unglamorous, wet and genuinely interesting.
Evening.
Back at the uma. If a sikerei is present and willing, this is when a healing ceremony might take place. It is not scheduled for visitors and it may not happen at all.
Base:
Same uma.
Booking logic:
Nothing.
Travel note:
Leeches are constant in the wet forest and harmless. Long socks over trouser legs and a lighter or a fingernail deal with them. Do not pull them off mid bite.
Day 6: Walk to a second valley
Morning.

A longer walk, commonly four to six hours, crossing ridges between river systems to a second uma. The trail is the same mud and log bridges, and the log bridges are the reason people fall. Take them slowly and use a stick.
Afternoon.
Arrive, wash in the river, and let the household get on with its day. The second uma usually feels easier than the first because you have stopped being startled by everything.
Evening.
Bow making, tattoo work or nothing at all, depending on the family and the day.
Base:
A second uma.
Booking logic:
Nothing.
Travel note:
This is the day people underestimate. If anyone in the group is struggling, say so in the morning and shorten it, because there is no way to shorten it halfway.
Day 7: Downriver to the coast
Morning.
Walk out to the river and take the canoe back down. Going downstream is faster and colder, and a dry bag matters more than it did going up.
Afternoon.
Back in Muara Siberut by mid afternoon. Shower, wash clothes that will not dry, and eat something that is not rice and sago.
Evening.
Settle the balance with your guide and confirm tomorrow's ferry is running.
Base:
Muara Siberut, same guesthouse.
Booking logic:
Ferry ticket for tomorrow, bought this afternoon.
Travel note:
Build today as the buffer. If the walk out takes longer than planned you still have the whole evening, and you have not gambled the crossing.
Day 8: The ferry back to Padang
Morning.
The Thursday sailing back to Padang, the same five to six hours in reverse. The return crossing often feels rougher because the afternoon wind gets up.
Afternoon.
Into Padang, into a hotel with hot water, and back into the world of mobile signal.
Evening.
Eat well. You have earned the second Padang dinner more than the first.
Base:
Padang.
Booking logic:
Book tonight's room before you sail, not after you land.
Travel note:
If the ferry is cancelled today, the next one is Saturday. That is precisely why the flight home is tomorrow evening and not tomorrow morning.
Day 9: Fly out, or keep going
Morning.
A slow morning in Padang. If the flight is late, the Bung Hatta memorial house or the fish market fill an hour each.
Afternoon.
Airport train or car to Minangkabau and out.
Or keep going.
Padang is also the gateway to the Minangkabau highlands, and adding four or five days turns this into a fuller Sumatra trip. Our
7-day West Sumatra route
through Bukittinggi and Harau Valley starts from exactly this airport.
What to book early, and what to keep flexible

Book the inland guiding well ahead, ideally a month or more. There are a limited number of experienced Siberut guides with established relationships in the Rereiket valleys, and in July, August and around the year end they are taken. Everything else on this trip can be arranged a day or two out.
Book early:
the guide and the inland days, your flights into Padang, and the first Padang night.
Book locally, a day ahead:
ferry tickets in both directions, Padang rooms after the first, and any airport transfer.
Do not book at all:
an itinerary that promises specific ceremonies, specific villages or a fixed number of hours of walking. Those are decided by weather and by whoever is at home when you arrive.
The one genuinely inflexible item is the return flight. Give yourself a full day in Padang after the ferry lands. Nine days works because of that day, and eight days does not.
Mistakes travellers make on Siberut
Flying in and sailing the same day.
The ferry leaves at seven in the morning and the first Jakarta arrivals do not reliably beat it. People do try, and people do miss it, and the next one is two days later.
Treating the ferry schedule as a guarantee.
It is a plan, and the sea overrules it. Every itinerary you build should survive one cancelled sailing.
Booking through someone who has never been.

Plenty of agencies resell Siberut trips without any relationship on the island, which usually means a rushed two nights, a lower share reaching the host family, and a guide who does not speak Mentawai.
Packing for a jungle instead of for rain.
It rains most days, all year. Two dry bags, rubber boots and quick-dry clothes matter far more than any technical gear.
Going for the photographs.

The tattoos and the sikerei are real, and they are also somebody's life rather than a set. Visitors who arrive curious about the forest and the household have a better week than visitors working through a shot list.
Underestimating the walking.
Four hours in Siberut mud is not four hours on a trail. If your group has mixed fitness, plan the shorter version from the start.
What to cut, adapt or upgrade
Cut to seven days.

Drop the second Padang day and one inland night. You lose the flight buffer, which is a real risk rather than a theoretical one, and you should only do it if you are already in Sumatra and not flying in the day before.
Cut the second uma.

Three nights in one valley with day walks out and back is a legitimate trip, and it is much easier on anyone who is not enjoying the mud. You lose the long ridge crossing, which is the hardest and best walk of the week.
Adapt for surf.

If waves are the point, Siberut is the wrong island. Sipora and the Pagais have the breaks and the camps, they sail on the other days of the week, and you should expect the Mentawai surfing levy on top of the package price.
Upgrade the Padang ends.
There are proper hotels in the city for the price of a mid-range room elsewhere, and after five nights on a floor the difference is worth more than usual.
Extend into Sumatra.
Two weeks lets you add the highlands or fly north. The
15-day Sumatra route
covers the classic north, and
Pulau Weh
is the natural reward at the end of a hard trip.
Do you have to pay the Mentawai surf tax if you do not surf?

The Mentawai levy is a surfing retribution, charged per surfer rather than per visitor, so a trekking trip on Siberut should not attract it. It runs to around Rp 2,000,000 per person, roughly USD 125, and covers up to fifteen consecutive days. It is set out in the Mentawai Islands Regency regional regulation on local taxes and levies, and the regency moved it to cashless collection during 2026.

Two caveats worth carrying. Enforcement varies by island and by year, and any guided walking inside Siberut National Park may carry its own park and guide fees, quoted separately. Ask your guide to itemise every fee before you go inland, and confirm the current position with the tourism office rather than with an old forum post.
Before you build this trip
Visa.

Most visitors enter Indonesia on a visa on arrival or e-VOA, around IDR 500,000 and roughly USD 35 as a working estimate, valid for thirty days and extendable once. Fees and rules change, so check the current official guidance before you fly.
The park and the reserve.

UNESCO designated Siberut a biosphere reserve in 1981, covering just over 403,000 hectares, and the western part of the island became Siberut National Park in 1993 at around 190,500 hectares. The island has been separated from Sumatra for at least half a million years, which is why so much of its wildlife is found nowhere else.
Money.

Cash only inland. Bring more than you think, in small notes, and confirm what proportion of your guiding fee reaches the host family. Paying the household directly for what you eat is normal and appreciated.
Health.
Malaria is present in the Mentawai. Take advice on prophylaxis well before you travel, bring repellent, and treat any cut in the forest immediately, because they infect quickly in this climate.
Language.
Indonesian will get you through Padang and the port. Inland, the language is Mentawai, and your guide is the interpreter as much as the navigator. That is the main reason to pay for a good one.
Connectivity.
Signal exists around Muara Siberut and vanishes upriver. Tell people at home you will be offline for four or five days, before you leave, rather than from the last bar of signal.
Final verdict

Siberut is the most demanding week in this collection and one of the few places left in western Indonesia where the effort of getting somewhere is still the price of admission. Nine days is the right length: enough for three nights inland with a real buffer at each end, and short enough that the ferry calendar still cooperates.

Go if you want rainforest, rivers and a household to sit with, and if you can accept mud, rain and a boat that may not sail. Do not go for waves, comfort or a tight schedule. Book a guide with genuine relationships on the island, pay properly, arrive curious, and it will be the trip you talk about for years.

faq.answer: Fly to Padang in West Sumatra, then take the Mentawai Fast passenger ferry to Muara Siberut. Siberut sailings are published for Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday, leaving around seven in the morning and taking roughly five to six hours with a stop at Sikabaluan. There is no airport on Siberut, so the ferry is the only scheduled way in and out.
faq.question: How do you get to Siberut Island?

faq.answer: Nine days from Padang is the shortest comfortable version. That gives you a buffer night in Padang before the crossing, one night at the port on each side, three nights inland in an uma, and a full day in Padang after you sail back. Because the ferry only runs every other day, trimming to seven days means gambling your flight home on a single sailing.
faq.question: How many days do you need on Siberut?

faq.answer: The Mentawai levy is charged per surfer rather than per visitor, so a trekking trip on Siberut should not attract it. It runs to around Rp 2,000,000 per person, roughly USD 125, and covers fifteen consecutive days. Enforcement varies, and guided walking inside Siberut National Park may carry separate park and guide fees, so ask your guide to itemise everything before you go inland.
faq.question: Do you have to pay the Mentawai surf tax if you are not surfing?

faq.answer: There is no reliable dry season. Rain falls year round on Siberut, so the practical variable is the sea state on the crossing rather than the weather on the island. Conditions are generally calmer between April and October, and the roughest crossings tend to come with the strong winds late in the year. Expect rain and mud whenever you go.
faq.question: What is the best time of year to visit Siberut?

faq.answer: As a working estimate, budget roughly USD 700 to 1,100 per person for nine days excluding international flights. The guided inland section is the largest single item, commonly quoted around USD 300 to 500 per person for three days and two nights based on two sharing. Ferry tickets run around Rp 350,000 to Rp 400,000 each way for foreign passengers. Prices change, so confirm before committing.
faq.question: How much does a Siberut trip cost?

faq.answer: Hosting visitors is an established and welcomed arrangement in the Rereiket valleys, provided it is set up through a guide with a genuine relationship there. Agree in advance what the host family receives directly, bring practical gifts such as sugar, coffee and batteries rather than money alone, and always ask before photographing anyone. Visitors who come curious about the forest and the household have a better time than those working through a shot list.
faq.question: Is it appropriate to stay with a Mentawai family?

faq.answer: Pack for constant rain rather than for a jungle expedition. Two dry bags, rubber boots bought in the Muara Siberut market, quick-dry clothes, long socks against leeches, a head torch, insect repellent and a basic first aid kit cover almost everything. Leave anything valuable in Padang, where most guesthouses will hold a bag at no charge.
